title: Persisted Queue First vs DB First
explain: Both patterns answer one question: where is the commit point, the moment the system tells the client OK and promises the event is never lost? In Queue First that is an append to a replicated log, and the DB is a downstream view. In DB First it is a database transaction, and the queue is only a wake-up hint. I pick by whether I need read-your-writes and write-time validation, or raw ingest throughput and replay.
model:
```
Queue First                               DB First
client -> append to Kafka (acks=all)      client -> DB txn: INSERT event (+ outbox)
       -> ack client   <- commit point            -> ack client    <- commit point
consumer: upsert DB (idempotent),         publish wake-up(entity_id)  (lossy ok)
          THEN commit offset              worker: lease entity, drain unprocessed rows
DB = materialized view                    sweeper / outbox repairs missed wake-ups
```

Queue First needs: `acks=all`, `min.insync.replicas >= 2`, no unclean leader election; DB write before offset commit; idempotent upsert by `event_id`; **retention longer than worst consumer lag**.

DB First needs: wake-up carries only `entity_id`; outbox or sweeper closes the dual-write gap; [lease](#/sd/f/lease) plus [fencing](#/sd/f/fencing-token) for a single writer.

**MQ is not storage:** ack-and-delete queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) are durable only in flight; only a replicated log (Kafka, Redpanda, Pulsar, Kinesis) can be a Queue First source of truth.

| | Queue First | DB First |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fits | telemetry, clickstream, append-only facts | chat, orders, payments, agent sessions |
| Weak at | read-your-writes, validation | ingest above DB txn rate |

Hybrid: DB First plus outbox/[change feed](#/sd/f/change-feed) into Kafka.

details.q: A team uses SQS as the source of truth: ack the client after enqueue, consumer writes DB later, replay last week if the schema is wrong. What is the flaw?
details.a: SQS deletes messages on consumption (and keeps them 14 days at most), so it cannot replay history or be queried by key; it only guarantees in-flight durability. Only a replicated log like Kafka can be the source of truth.

details.q: Why must the consumer upsert to the DB before committing the offset?
details.a: A crash between the two steps then re-reads and re-applies the event (at-least-once), which an idempotent upsert absorbs. The reverse order loses the event on a crash, since Kafka thinks it was consumed but the DB never got it.

details.q: Producers write 20,000 events/s, the consumer maxes at 25,000/s and was down 2 hours. How long to catch up?
details.a: Backlog is 144 million events, net drain is 5,000/s, so 28,800 s, about 8 hours. It also means retention must exceed the worst lag, or acked events are deleted before they reach the DB: real data loss.

details.q: A client resends event E after a timeout, and ingest uses an idempotent producer. How many copies can land in the log?
details.a: Possibly two. The Kafka idempotent producer dedupes only retries within one producer session; a resend is a new append. Clients send a stable event_id, and every consumer dedupes on it (unique constraint or upsert). Redis SETNX at ingest only reduces duplicates because it is not in the same transaction.

details.q: A money-transfer app must reject insufficient balance immediately and show the new balance next screen. Which pattern?
details.a: DB First: validate and commit in one transaction, optionally emit an outbox event. Queue First cannot validate at append time, so the client sees OK and the failure arrives later in the consumer.

details.q: In DB First, the process crashes after the commit but before publishing the wake-up. How is it repaired?
details.a: Write an outbox row in the same transaction and relay it (relay or CDC), or run a sweeper that re-enqueues entities with unprocessed rows. Publishing before the commit would create wake-ups for data that may not exist.

details.q: Why should the wake-up not carry the payload?
details.a: Duplicated or reordered messages would execute the command twice or out of order. Carry only the entity_id and read the current state from the DB; duplicate wake-ups merge into one drain.

details.q: What do real systems usually do?
details.a: Mix: interactive path DB First for read-your-writes and validation, then outbox plus CDC into Kafka for fan-out, analytics and replay; or route by data type, core events DB First and telemetry Queue First. The agent-session case is DB First with a queue wake-up to a worker holding a lease.

prompts.q: Explain the difference between the two patterns using the commit point.
points: Commit point: when you say OK and promise not to lose the event
Queue First: log append, DB is a materialized view
DB First: DB transaction, queue is a lossy wake-up hint
Only a replicated log qualifies as a Queue First source of truth

prompts.q: List what you must get right to make Queue First safe.
points: acks=all, min.insync.replicas at least 2, no unclean election
DB write before offset commit, idempotent upsert
event_id from the client, dedupe in every consumer
Retention greater than worst lag, alert on lag
Accept weak read-your-writes and write-time validation

prompts.q: List what you must get right to make DB First safe.
points: Single commit point in the DB transaction
Outbox or sweeper for the dual-write gap
Wake-up carries only entity_id and can be merged
Lease plus fencing for a single writer

prompts.q: Pick a pattern for clickstream, then for a chat or agent session, and justify each.
points: Clickstream: append-only, high volume, lag tolerable, many consumers: Queue First
Chat or agent session: read-your-writes, query by entity, validation: DB First
Mention hybrid with outbox and CDC for fan-out
Decision questions: read back immediately, validation, write rate, replay needs
